chain.note: Proposed causal step; human GWAS establishes locus association but not this mechanism.

falsification.description: Engineer the human MEIS1 RLS-risk haplotype in isogenic circadian-competent neural cultures or a knock-in mouse and measure rest-phase neural activity, sleep timing, and limb movements; the hypothesis is falsified if the verified allele has no effect on circadian programs or rest-phase motor activity.
falsification.system: isogenic neural cultures and MEIS1 risk-haplotype knock-in mouse

hypotheses.mechanism: RLS-associated variants map very strongly to MEIS1, while disruption of the mouse orthologue produces an abnormal circadian sleep/wake cycle. The falsifiable claim is that the risk locus changes MEIS1-dependent neural timing programs, increasing motor or sensory symptoms specifically during the normal rest phase; positional mapping alone does not establish the causal variant, direction of expression change, or responsible cell type.
hypotheses.title: MEIS1 risk variation promotes RLS by disrupting circadian sleep–wake control

chain.note: Proposed mechanism connecting the associated locus to disease.

object.label: restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements

falsification.description: Restore BTBD9 selectively in somatosensory neurons of Btbd9-deficient mice and quantify sleep-stage electrophysiology and periodic limb movements; failure of verified rescue to normalize either readout would falsify the proposed somatosensory sleep-circuit mechanism.

readout.label: sleep-stage sensory electrophysiology and periodic limb movements

hypotheses.mechanism: BTBD9 has replicated human association with RLS and periodic limb movements, and Btbd9-deficient mice show abnormal sleep behavior, nervous-system electrophysiology, and somatosensory-cortex morphology. The causal hypothesis is that altered BTBD9 function destabilizes sensory gating during sleep, generating uncomfortable limb sensations and periodic movements; the molecular substrate and direction of the risk allele remain unresolved.
hypotheses.title: BTBD9 risk variation promotes RLS through sleep and somatosensory-circuit dysfunction

chain.note: Proposed disease mechanism; the available animal phenotype is not specific to RLS.

falsification.description: Introduce the PTPRD RLS-risk haplotype into isogenic human motor-neuron/sensory-neuron circuits and test spontaneous activity during low-input rest-like conditions; the hypothesis is falsified if the verified haplotype produces no reproducible electrophysiologic or motor-output change.

hypotheses.mechanism: Independent RLS GWAS records map strongly to PTPRD, and Ptprd-null mice have impaired swimming, supporting a role in neural motor function. The falsifiable claim is that an RLS risk allele changes PTPRD activity in a motor or sensorimotor circuit, increasing rest-associated motor disinhibition; however, impaired swimming is nonspecific and the GWAS assignments remain positional.
hypotheses.title: PTPRD risk variation promotes RLS by impairing motor-circuit function

chain.note: Proposed modifier mechanism; direct human genetic support was not found.

falsification.description: Perturb ACO1 in an adult neural lineage while controlling systemic iron, then measure brain iron and rest-phase limb movements; the hypothesis is falsified if verified ACO1 disruption changes neither neural iron handling nor the movement phenotype.

readout.label: brain iron and rest-phase limb movements

hypotheses.mechanism: Loss of mouse Aco1 causes abnormal iron homeostasis, making ACO1 a biologically plausible link to the iron-sensitive component of RLS. However, the GWAS Catalog reports no ACO1–RLS association, so this is better framed as a rare-variant, environmental-interaction, or downstream modifier hypothesis rather than a common inherited RLS locus.
hypotheses.title: ACO1 dysfunction may modify RLS through disturbed iron homeostasis
